So I want to start a problem series - and if it works, a marathon - that includes all sorts of hard problems that have to do with surviving the outdoors. Be creative, like stranded on a island or throwing stones to defend yourself.



I'll start with a classic:

P1: Save yourself from poisonThis came from a Ted-ed video:

You are walking in the forest when you get bitten by a snake. You see that the snake is the kind that kills you after a few hours. You are far away from help, and the only way to get the cure is from the very rare frogs that happen to live in the forest. But here's the twist: only the males give the cure. There is a 60% chance a frog is male. You see, with a burst of luck, that in front of you is a frog, exactly the one you need. However, you do not know it's gender. At that time, you hear the female's distinctive croak behind you, and see two frogs sitting there. You know at least one of them is female, but not if there is a male. You can only get the cure from either the frog you saw first or the two frogs behind you. What is the probability you survive in each case, and which one should you chose?

topics.title: Why an odd number plus an even number equals an odd number
topics.text:
I have never written a single proof in my life, and today, I wrote a proof on why an odd number plus an even number equals an odd number.  Since this is my first time, can someone help me catch mistakes in "proof-writing" in general?



Why does an Even Number Plus an Odd Number Equal an Odd Number?An even number is written as $2n$, since two times any number $n$ is even.

An odd number is written as $2n+1$, since $1$ added to any even number is odd.  We know this because we know that odd and even numbers alternate.



So, an even number plus an odd number equals

\begin{align*}
2n+2n+1\\
4n+1\\
\end{align*}Any number multiplied by $4$ is even.  Like before, $1$ plus any even number is odd.

Therefore, an even plus an odd number equals an odd number.

topics.title: Envelope Game
topics.text:
I thought it would be fun to share some problems I enjoy here. Here's a fun one I came by recently.



Please use hide tags if you include a solution or answer. But there is no need for hide tags if you're just discussing.



--------------------



[quote=A game]

I have two envelopes, each containing a random amount of money from $1 to $100.



First, I hand you an envelope and you open it. You can choose to accept or reject the money.



Next, I hand you the second envelope and you open it. You can only accept this money if it is more than what you have already accepted.



For example, if I hand you $31 and you accept, then hand you $18, you cannot accept the second envelope. But if I hand you $31 and you accept, then hand you $40, you can accept again.

[/quote]



Assuming your goal is to win as much money as possible, what is your strategy for this game? What are your ideas?



A stretchWhat if we upped the number of envelopes to 3? You still cannot accept anything smaller than what you already got. For example, you can accept 8, 10, 11 but not 8, 11, 10.

topics.title: Utilizing Base 10 Algebraically

Find first digit

Find 2nd digit if possible

topics.title: Michigan Mathcounts
topics.text:
Hello AOPS,



I was just at Michigan State Mathcounts this weekend, and Reagan Choi (again) placed 1st, and will be advancing to nationals, as will the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th. I also want to congratulate the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th, as they did very good in the countdown round too. Last year he placed 5th at nationals, and I think he will do even better this year as well. My sister competed, and did well, but not quite enough to get into the countdown round, she has next year still. I got to see Regan Choi; I have heard all about him. He is very good at math, he answers the questions in 3-5 seconds! Michigan did well, and I think Michigan's team well do good at Mathcounts Nats.



Congratulations again to Reagan Choi and Michigan Mathcounts Competitors! :clap2:

topics.title: Problem of the Day #4
topics.text:
Bob is captured by aliens. Bob has acquired a map of the alien ship somehow. Bob knows that when he tries to escape, the aliens will chase after him. So, Bob can only go down to the left or the right when stopping at a corner, and cannot backtrack. Bob suffers from short-term memory loss, so he will not remember the map and will run in a random direction each corner. There are 8 exits, but what Bob does not know is that 7 of them have a death trap - only exit K has a safe haven for Bob. What is the probability Bob survives?

Difficulty: This problem is stupid couldn't think of a good one
